description: Sygnition is a Space Apps team building a functional tool to unify historical fire records from multiple satellite sensors. Open to new members looking to collaborate and build.
summary:
UFRS (Unified Fire Reconnaissance System) is an interactive web platform that combines active fire hotspot data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites into a single, clear view for forestry officials and emergency responders.

During active wildfires, raw satellite feeds are difficult to interpret because multiple satellites detect the same fire at different resolutions, times, and confidence scales—creating duplicate hotspots and inflated fire intensity numbers.

UFRS solves this by automatically merging overlapping detections into unified fire events, calibrating fire intensity across satellites, and organizing passes by local fire day. Using an interactive 3D globe and timeline, responders can track how fires evolve day and night, separate persistent forest wildfires from short-lived agricultural burns or industrial heat sources, and export clean, decision-ready fire reports in one click.
details:
1. What UFRS Does & Why It Matters When a wildfire breaks out, forestry officers and emergency responders rely on satellite hotspot data to decide where to send crews. Today, NASA's FIRMS platform streams detections from multiple satellites—MODIS (Terra & Aqua, 1 km resolution) and VIIRS (NOAA-20 & NOAA-21, 375 m resolution)—each using different pixel sizes, confidence scales, and timestamps.

Because of these differences, a single 1 km² wildfire can appear as 15 to 45 overlapping detections in a single day, inflating fire counts by more than 11x and triple-counting fire intensity. UFRS (Unified Fire Reconnaissance System) turns that noisy, conflicting raw data into one clear, decision-ready picture:

  • Find real wildfires fast: Automatically separates dangerous, overnight-burning forest wildfires from short-lived daytime crop stubble burns, volcanoes, and industrial heat sources.
  • See true fire size and strength: Combines overlapping satellite detections into single, calibrated 1 km fire events with accurate Fire Radiative Power (MW).
  • Act immediately: Lets responders explore any region on an interactive 3D globe or 2D map, scrub through Day and Night satellite passes, and download a clean, jargon-free CSV report in one click.

2. How It Works (4 Simple Stages)

  • Stage 1 — Multi-Satellite Data Collection: UFRS fetches fire detections in 5-day batches from MODIS, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 (excluding Suomi-NPP due to its November 2026 feed discontinuation). It automatically switches between Near Real-Time data for active fires and Standard Processing data for historical context and known static heat sources (like volcanoes and factories).
  • Stage 2 — Aligning Day & Night Fire Cycles: Satellites pass overhead around 1:30 PM and 1:30 AM local time. Standard UTC timestamps often split a single day's afternoon ignition and its overnight burn across two different calendar dates. UFRS shifts timestamps to a Local Solar Fire Day (resetting at 4:00 AM local time, when fires are quietest) so each daytime pass and its matching overnight pass stay together.
  • Stage 3 — Merging Duplicates & Calibrating Intensity: UFRS groups all detections within 1 km on the same fire day, anchoring on the hottest fire cores first. To prevent double- or triple-counting energy, it sums fire power within each satellite sensor family first and then averages across the satellites that saw the fire. It also translates MODIS numeric scores (0–100) and VIIRS letters (Low / Nominal / High) into one unified confidence scale.
  • Stage 4 — Interactive 3D Globe & One-Click Export: Responders can view either raw satellite footprints or harmonized 1 km fire events on a 3D Globe or 2D Map, step through a 10-day Day/Night timeline, and export a standardized 16-column CSV built for field teams.

3. Real-World Validation (2024 California Park Fire) We tested UFRS across a 10-day window (July 22–31, 2024) during California's Park Fire:

  • 17,817 raw pixels merged cleanly into 1,595 confirmed 1 km fire events (11.17x noise reduction).
  • Eliminated a 2.61x energy overcount, calibrating 1,078,963.8 MW of raw overlapping sums down to 413,051.8 MW of true radiative power.
  • 74.0% of fire events were independently confirmed by 2 or more satellites, and UFRS pinpointed the 24.6% of persistent Day + Night fire cores driving overnight spread.

4. Intended Impact & Creativity Most fire dashboards simply plot raw satellite dots on top of each other. UFRS bridges the gap between raw space-agency telemetry and real-world forestry operations—giving non-technical responders a fast, honest, and physically accurate view of where fires are actually growing, whether in California's forests or North India's agricultural belts.

5. Tools, Languages & Hardware Used

  • Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS (3D Globe & 2D Map), Zustand, and pnpm.
  • Backend & Data Science: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy (spatial clustering), and Matplotlib, prototyped in Google Colab and JupyterLab.
